analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering every U.S. resident with no deductibles or copays.
analysis.headline: The Medicare for All Act of 2017 was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2017 but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, employer insurance, ACA exchanges, TRICARE, and federal employee coverage with a single national health insurance program run by the Department of Health and Human Services. Every U.S. resident would be covered for hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, mental health, reproductive care, and long-term care, with no deductibles or copays except a capped annual charge for some prescription drugs. It would phase in over four years, first covering children, then lowering the Medicare age to 55, 45, and 35 during the transition. Private insurers could no longer sell coverage that duplicates the program's benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, including people currently uninsured, underinsured, or stuck with high deductibles, would get comprehensive coverage with no premiums tied to income, no deductibles, and no copays for most care. People with employer insurance would no longer lose coverage when they change jobs, and the bill bans balance billing and ends surprise out-of-network charges.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a universal entitlement: every U.S. resident is entitled to health care benefits, with automatic enrollment at birth and at immigration [S3].

Covers hospital services, ambulatory care, primary and preventive care, prescription drugs, medical devices, mental health and substance abuse treatment, lab services, reproductive and maternity care, pediatrics, oral health, audiology, vision, and rehabilitative services [S3].

Bars cost-sharing — deductibles, coinsurance, and copays — for covered benefits, with limited exceptions including an evidence-based prescription drug cost-sharing schedule capped at $200 per person per year, and prohibits balance billing [S3].
Phases in over four years: children under 19 covered in year one, a transitional Medicare buy-in for adults starting at age 55 and dropping to 45 then 35, and full implementation in year four [S3].
Requires the Secretary to negotiate prices for prescription drugs annually and to run a formulary that promotes generic drugs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the program through a new Universal Medicare Trust Fund; the bill text establishes the fund's revenue sources but leaves the specifics of new taxes open. Private health insurers would lose their core market, brand-name drug makers would face government-negotiated prices, employers could no longer offer duplicative health benefits, and workers' compensation carriers would have to reimburse the program for work-injury care.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not spell out the new taxes that would finance the program; it creates a trust fund fed by revenue attributed to its amendments, so the actual cost to taxpayers was left to later action [S3].

It would be unlawful for private insurers to sell or employers to provide coverage duplicating the program's benefits, so the roughly 155 million Americans with employer coverage at the time would have had to move into the new government program, a major disruption of existing arrangements [S3].

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office was never asked to score the bill, so there is no official estimate of its total cost, savings, or net effect on national health spending; outside estimates of comparable single-payer plans run to tens of trillions of dollars over a decade.

Health insurance industry jobs would be eliminated; the bill sets aside up to 1 percent of the program budget for up to five years to assist displaced workers who administer the health insurance system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: universal coverage, the end of deductibles, copays, networks, and balance billing, and coverage expanded to dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care. The cost is also large, and the bill itself dodges the hardest question — who pays and how — by creating a trust fund without specifying the taxes to fill it. An honest supporter would concede that financing would require significant new taxes and that dismantling employer-based insurance is a disruption most Americans have never experienced.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced the bill in September 2017 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on September 13, 2017, with 16 Democratic cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and employers that fund group health coverage were better off because the bill never moved; the status quo of employer-based and mixed public-private insurance was preserved without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug makers, and the status quo

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its first Senate single-payer listing a bloc of Democratic caucus members.

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against single-payer legislation, which would eliminate their core business of selling primary health coverage.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was an independent who caucuses with them; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding 52 Senate seats and chairing every committee, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill bans insurers from selling coverage duplicating the program's benefits, ending their primary business of selling basic health insurance to individuals and employers; only coverage for extras not in the program would remain. Insurers' gatekeeping role over Americans' access to care and their roughly trillion-dollar-a-year revenue stream would be eliminated.

The Secretary would negotiate drug prices annually and run a formulary promoting generics, replacing today's system where drug makers set prices largely unchecked across many payers. The program's enormous bargaining power would directly cut their revenue on any drug it covers.

Providers would be paid under Medicare-style fee schedules rather than higher negotiated private insurance rates, cutting payments at many hospitals, but they would gain guaranteed payment for every patient, an end to unpaid care, and a single set of billing rules instead of dozens of insurers.

Employers would be barred from offering benefits that duplicate the program, removing a benefit they use to recruit and retain workers but also relieving them of premium contributions that cost many large employers billions a year. The bill does not specify the taxes that would replace employer spending, so the net effect on any employer depends on financing not in the text.

The bill requires workers' compensation insurers to reimburse the Universal Medicare Program for the cost of medical care for work-related injuries, ending their role in covering workplace injury treatment.
